title: Reduced multisensory imagery in autism: a preregistered test of Arnold et al. (2026) in an independent public sample, with ADHD as a comparison group
description: [DRAFT FOR IVAN TO REWRITE] Arnold et al. (2026) reported that autistic adults describe less vivid mental imagery across the senses, and are more often unable to imagine smells and tastes, but are not more often unable to picture images. These findings come from one sample. We test them in a second, independent public dataset (New et al., 2026, Study 2; N = 1,003), where participants reported whether they had been diagnosed with, or strongly suspected, autism, ADHD or other neurodevelopmental conditions. The source paper analysed only the combined any-condition group. We compare 150 participants who ticked autism and 84 who ticked ADHD only with 749 who reported no condition. The main tests are, in fixed order: lower overall imagery in autism; more absent smell imagery; more absent taste imagery. ADHD serves as a comparison to test whether any pattern is specific to autism. Decision rules, including how a failed replication will be interpreted, are fixed in advance. No autism- or ADHD-specific imagery comparison has been computed before registration.

responses.72-2:
Arnold et al. (2026, Consciousness and Cognition 143, 104085) surveyed 327 adults who reported a formal autism diagnosis and compared them with an earlier comparison sample. The autistic group reported less vivid imagery across modalities on average. It was not more likely to report absent visual imagery, but was more likely to report being unable to imagine smell and taste. These claims have not been tested in an independent sample.

New et al. (2026, Cortex 201, 119-136), Study 2, is an independent public sample (OSF 2bdn6) that measured imagery in eight modalities. It also asked whether participants had been diagnosed with, or strongly suspected they had, a neurodevelopmental condition, followed by a checklist of conditions. The source paper analysed only the combined any-condition indicator. It did not analyse autism or ADHD separately.

Research question 1: In New et al. Study 2, do participants who ticked autism show Arnold et al.'s pattern: lower overall imagery, and more frequent absence of smell and taste imagery?
Research question 2: Is any such pattern specific to autism, or is it also seen in participants who ticked ADHD but not autism?
responses.72-4:
Definitions. "ASD group" = participants who ticked Autism Spectrum Disorder on the checklist, with or without other conditions. "ADHD-only group" = ticked ADHD but not autism. "Reference group" = answered No to the neurodevelopmental question. Directional predictions come from Arnold et al. (2026).

Primary hypotheses (tested in this fixed order; see Statistical models):
H1 (general imagery shift): the ASD group has a lower general imagery composite than the reference group, adjusting for age and recorded sex/gender. The composite is the average of six modalities shared with Arnold et al.: visual, auditory, smell, taste, touch, movement.
H2a (absent smell imagery): the ASD group has higher odds of absent smell imagery (the lowest possible smell score) than the reference group.
H2b (absent taste imagery): as H2a, for taste.

Secondary hypotheses:
S1: the ASD-reference gap is larger for smell and taste than for visual imagery (predicted direction: larger gap for smell and taste). Also an overall test of whether the gap differs across the six modalities.
S2: the ASD and ADHD-only groups differ on the general imagery composite (no directional prediction). This is the specificity test.
S3: odds of absent visual imagery, ASD vs reference (no directional prediction; Arnold et al. reported no increase, so a null result would agree with them).
S4: the S1 smell-and-taste-versus-visual comparison for ADHD-only vs reference (no directional prediction).
responses.72-7:
Main dataset: New et al. (2026), Study 2, file Analyses/Exp3.1020.txt in the public OSF project 2bdn6 (osf.io/2bdn6). Local copy SHA-256: 6abd7a36b3e89c20936c295f5a8569aea545b49562f8ef388a057a5e75462bdd.

Sample: 1,020 source rows. Applying the source paper's attention check (nbact score of 3 or more) leaves 1,003, matching the published N. Group counts after the attention check: reference 749; ASD 150 (46 of whom also ticked ADHD); ADHD-only 84; other conditions only (e.g., dyslexia, dyspraxia) 20; answered Yes but ticked nothing 0. The 20 other-condition-only participants are excluded from all models.

Comparison dataset: Arnold et al. (2026), public analysis code with embedded response arrays (UQ eSpace, DOI 10.48610/57f325b). Local archive SHA-256: 48b3eaf7a9e3fbc97fb8db5d9e2d6306c3f8df2d9197d1ca55c61dfecf4394e3. Used for side-by-side comparison only (327 formally diagnosed autistic participants vs 327 comparison participants).
responses.72-14: New et al.: https://osf.io/2bdn6/ (public OSF project). Arnold et al.: https://doi.org/10.48610/57f325b (UQ eSpace, public).
responses.72-16: New et al. (2026) paper: doi:10.1016/j.cortex.2026.04.019; data: osf.io/2bdn6. Arnold et al. (2026) paper: doi:10.1016/j.concog.2026.104085; data: doi:10.48610/57f325b.
responses.72-20: Data were collected by the original authors; we did not collect any data. New et al. Study 2 was an online questionnaire study; the file contains Prolific identifiers, indicating recruitment through Prolific. Participants completed imagery questionnaires for eight modalities and an attention check (nbact). The neurodevelopmental items were: "Have you ever been diagnosed with, or strongly suspected to have, a neurodevelopmental disorder such as Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD), Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD), or a learning disability?" (No/Yes), followed by a multi-select checklist (ASD, ADHD, Dyslexia, Dyscalculia, Dysgraphia, Language Disorder, Dyspraxia, Other). Wording was taken from the archived questionnaire PDF in the OSF project (Study 2, pages 3-4). Full procedures are described in New et al. (2026) and Arnold et al. (2026).
responses.72-24:
Imagery scores in New et al. Study 2 are sums of five items rated 1-7 (range 5-35; higher = more vivid). Crosswalk to Arnold et al.'s six modality columns: visual = image; auditory = sound; smell = smell; taste = taste; touch = touch; movement = motor. Study 2's emotion, voice and interoception (intstate) scores have no Arnold counterpart and are exploratory only.

Group variables: isneurodev (0/1 answer to the gate question) and neurodev2 (comma-separated checklist). Covariates: age (years) and sex (source codes 0, 1 and O; the three participants coded O are kept as their own category).

Absent imagery for a modality = a score of 5 (all five items at the minimum), which is New et al.'s own definition in their analysis script. For Arnold et al., absent imagery = a score of 0, their own strict-absence definition.
responses.72-33:
Exposure: group (ASD, ADHD-only, reference), defined from isneurodev and neurodev2 as described under Hypotheses. Diagnosis and strong suspicion cannot be separated in this dataset, so the exposure is self-reported diagnosed or strongly suspected autism. Arnold et al. required a self-reported formal diagnosis; we report this difference as a limitation.

Outcomes:
1. Modality scores for visual, auditory, smell, taste, touch and movement imagery. Each modality is standardized against the reference group's mean and standard deviation (SD).
2. General imagery composite: the average of the six standardized modality scores, re-standardized so that the reference group has mean 0 and SD 1. Group differences are therefore in reference-group SD units. Arnold et al.'s data are standardized the same way against their comparison group.
3. Absent imagery indicators for smell, taste and visual imagery (score = 5).

Covariates: age (linear) and recorded sex/gender. No other covariates. Education and occupation are not adjusted for, because they may be affected by the exposure and Arnold et al. did not adjust for them.
responses.72-35: One participant has missing age. They are excluded from age-adjusted models (complete-case analysis) and kept in unadjusted descriptive statistics. No imputation, because missingness is below 0.1%. Imagery scores have no missing values in the source file; if any were found, that person's composite would be treated as missing (no partial composites).
responses.72-37: Individual participants. The modality-profile models (S1, S4) use six scores per participant, with standard errors clustered by participant.
responses.72-39: No outlier exclusions. Scores outside the valid 5-35 range would stop the analysis (the loader fails) rather than being removed.
responses.72-44: New et al. (2026) published analyses of these data, including the prevalence of aphantasia and hyperphantasia by modality and comparisons using the combined any-condition neurodevelopmental indicator. They did not report autism-specific or ADHD-specific analyses. Arnold et al. (2026) published their own analyses of their data; their prevalence comparisons used a subset of 242 autistic participants with AQ scores of 26 or more, whereas we use all 327.
responses.72-46:
The author has read both source papers. Arnold et al.'s arrays have been fully reanalysed (all 327 vs 327, and the 242-person subset). Those results, including the effect sizes used for the power analysis, are known.

New et al. Study 2 has previously been used by the author for an unrelated analysis of current neurological/psychiatric treatment. One model in that analysis regressed the combined any-condition neurodevelopmental indicator on visual and nonvisual imagery (visual OR 0.86, 95% CI 0.70-1.05; nonvisual OR 0.89, 95% CI 0.73-1.08). That indicator mixes autism, ADHD and learning conditions, but it partly hints at the direction of H1, and we disclose it for that reason.

For this plan, only structural information from New et al. Study 2 was inspected: questionnaire wording, checklist codes and group counts. No autism-specific or ADHD-specific comparison of any imagery score, composite or absence rate has been computed. The analysis code is locked: it will not run until the plan file is frozen (its SHA-256 recorded) and a registration link is supplied, and the pre-registration tests used synthetic data only.
responses.72-49:
All models are fitted once, as specified. All estimates are reported with 95% confidence intervals whatever their significance.

Primary analyses.
H1: ordinary least squares (OLS) regression of the general imagery composite on an ASD indicator (ASD vs reference), age and sex/gender, with HC3 robust standard errors. One-sided t test of the ASD coefficient (predicted below 0).
H2a and H2b: logistic regression of absent smell (taste) imagery on the ASD indicator, age and sex/gender, with robust (White) standard errors. One-sided test that the odds ratio is above 1. If the ordinary logistic fit is separated or singular, Firth bias-reduced logistic regression is used instead.
Sparse-event rule: if fewer than 10 participants in the analysed pair have absent imagery for that modality, H2 instead uses an unadjusted exact (conditional maximum-likelihood) odds ratio, with an exact 95% CI and a one-sided Fisher exact test.
Error control: fixed-sequence testing at one-sided alpha = .05 in the order H1, H2a, H2b. A hypothesis counts as confirmatory only if every earlier hypothesis was supported. Later hypotheses are still estimated and reported, labelled non-confirmatory. This keeps the chance of any false positive across the three at 5%. H1 comes first because it is Arnold et al.'s broadest claim and the best-powered test.

Secondary analyses (two-sided; Holm correction across five p-values).
S1: long-format model with six standardized modality scores per participant. Predictors: ASD indicator, modality indicators (visual as reference), ASD-by-modality interactions, age and sex/gender. Standard errors clustered by participant. Tested quantities: (a) the smell-and-taste-versus-visual contrast, the average of the ASD-by-smell and ASD-by-taste interactions; (b) the 5-degree-of-freedom Wald test of all ASD-by-modality interactions.
S2: OLS of the general composite on ASD and ADHD-only indicators (reference group as baseline), age and sex/gender, with HC3 standard errors. Tested quantity: the ASD minus ADHD-only difference. The ADHD-only vs reference estimate is reported alongside, without a separate test.
S3: as H2, for absent visual imagery (two-sided).
S4: as S1, for ADHD-only vs reference (smell-and-taste-versus-visual contrast).

Comparison with Arnold et al. The same H1 and S1 models are fitted to Arnold et al.'s data (all 327 vs 327, standardized against their comparison group). The two studies' estimates are shown side by side, with a two-sided z test of their difference. They are not pooled: two cohorts with different instruments, recruitment and diagnostic definitions do not justify a single combined estimate.

Software: Python 3.12+ (NumPy, pandas, SciPy); code in src/aphantasia/p5.py of the project repository [ADD PUBLIC REPOSITORY LINK]. Complete plan: preregistration.md, SHA-256 a6922215db899d7583cd000ca09ecdf7ac151fd9161960c9a08b91d5eb040287.
responses.72-51: H1 effect: adjusted mean difference in the general imagery composite, in reference-group SD units. H2 effect: adjusted odds ratio for absent imagery. For planning, Arnold et al.'s all-327 effects were: general composite -0.22 SD; smell-and-taste-versus-visual contrast -0.13 SD; absent smell 7.3% vs 2.4% (odds ratio about 3.2); absent taste 6.1% vs 2.4% (odds ratio about 2.6). Published effects tend to be overestimated, so half of Arnold et al.'s effect is treated as the realistic lower scenario.
responses.72-53:
The sample size is fixed by the existing data (ASD 150, ADHD-only 84, reference 749). Power was computed before registration using only Arnold et al.'s effect sizes and within-person correlations plus the New et al. group sizes. One-sided alpha = .05.
H1, ASD vs reference: 0.79 at Arnold et al.'s effect; 0.34 at half that effect.
H1, ASD without ADHD: 0.67 at Arnold's effect; 0.27 at half.
S1 contrast: 0.63 at Arnold's effect; 0.25 at half.
H2a/H2b: 0.87 if the odds ratio is 3; 0.46 if it is 2. This assumes the reference group's absence rate equals Arnold et al.'s comparison-group rate (2.4%).
Because power is modest if the true effect is smaller than Arnold et al. found, the inference criteria below define in advance how a non-significant result is interpreted.
responses.72-55:
H1 is interpreted with three prespecified outcomes, using the "small telescopes" approach (Simonsohn, 2015). d33 is the effect size that Arnold et al.'s design had 33% power to detect, computed from the standard error of their adjusted H1 estimate (about 0.12 reference SD).
1. Replicated: H1 one-sided p below .05. Reported as consistent with Arnold et al.: lower overall imagery in autism.
2. Informative non-replication: H1 not supported, and our estimate is significantly closer to zero than -d33 (one-sided p below .05). Reported as an effect too small for Arnold et al.'s design to have detected reliably.
3. Inconclusive: neither of the above. We report the interval and the effect sizes it cannot rule out.

H2: replication of Arnold et al.'s absence finding requires confirmatory support under the fixed-sequence rule. Otherwise the odds-ratio interval is reported alongside Arnold et al.'s odds ratios.
S2 (specificity): the pattern is called autism-specific only if the ASD minus ADHD-only confidence interval excludes 0. An ADHD estimate near zero is not, by itself, evidence of specificity.
No causal claims: all estimates are associations in a self-selected online sample.
responses.72-57: Logistic models automatically switch to Firth bias-reduced regression if the ordinary fit is separated, singular or does not converge. Absence outcomes with fewer than 10 events use the exact odds ratio described under Statistical models. Robust (HC3 or White) standard errors are used throughout, so non-constant variance does not require a model change. If a model still cannot be estimated, it is reported as not estimable, with the reason; it is not replaced by a different model. Any departure from this plan is logged in a dated deviations file stating whether results had been seen, and reported in the paper.
responses.72-59:
Sensitivity analyses (all reported; they do not replace the primary results):
1. H1, H2a and H2b restricted to autistic participants who did not also tick ADHD (n = 104) vs reference.
2. H1 using the unstandardized average of the six raw scores (5-35 points).
3. H1 restricted to ages 18-30, the source study's eligibility range.
4. H1 without covariates.
5. S1 with added age-by-modality and sex/gender-by-modality terms.
responses.72-61: Unadjusted Hedges' g (ASD vs reference; ADHD-only vs reference) for each of the six shared modalities (descriptive), and for emotion, voice and interoception imagery (exploratory; no hypothesis tests). Counts of absent imagery by group and modality, with cells smaller than 5 shown as "fewer than 5". Any other analysis will be labelled exploratory in the paper.
responses.72-29: None. This is an observational secondary analysis of existing data.
